blocks.content: 3. Real, Common Record Types
A, CNAME, and Alias are the real, most commonly used record types, each serving a genuinely different, real, practical DNS purpose.
An A record points a real, specific name directly at an IP address, CNAME points at another, real domain name instead.
An Alias record, an AWS-specific, real extension, points directly at an AWS resource, a load balancer, for instance, without needing a real, static IP at all.
Understanding these real, common types is genuinely sufficient for the large majority of real, practical DNS configuration needs.

blocks.content: 6. TTL: How Long an Answer Is Cached
blocks.text: 6. TTL: How Long an Answer Is Cached

blocks.content: Time to Live, TTL, determines how long a real DNS answer is cached, genuinely, elsewhere, before a client asks again for a fresh, real answer.
An alias record's TTL is managed automatically by AWS, other, real record types set this explicitly, a real, practical value worth understanding.
A genuinely low TTL means real changes propagate quickly, but genuinely increases real, ongoing DNS query volume, a real, practical tradeoff worth understanding.
This small, real detail matters most during an actual, planned migration, where DNS needs to genuinely change quickly and reliably.
A genuinely reasonable default, 300 seconds, works well for most, real, everyday records, worth lowering deliberately only around a real, planned change.
This connects directly back to the real, upfront planning discipline already covered throughout this entire course, applied here to DNS specifically.

blocks.text: 7. Reading an Existing Zone With a Data Source

This connects directly back to the general principle already covered, reading existing, real infrastructure rather than genuinely recreating it unnecessarily.

blocks.content: 8. A Real, Common Mistake
A real, genuinely low TTL, left in place long term, unnecessarily, is a real, common mistake, causing needlessly high, real, ongoing DNS query volume.
This often happens because a low TTL was set deliberately for a real, specific, past migration, and simply never raised again once that migration genuinely finished.
The honest fix is revisiting real TTL values after any real, planned change, raising them back once fast propagation is genuinely no longer needed.
This small, real detail is easy to overlook, worth adding to a genuine, real post-migration checklist for any future, similar change.
